summary: Describes a framework for composing and aggregating IP Performance Metrics across time and space, so measurements of parts of a path can be combined into a view of the whole. It is the basis for follow-on documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5835 explains how to combine network measurements across time or across parts of a network. A combined result estimates a whole-path or longer-period measurement, and its assumptions and possible error need to be stated.

questions: what is spatial aggregation of metrics
subtitle: A framework for estimating larger network or time-span metrics from smaller measurements.

tldr.problem: A large network cannot measure every path, and operators may need both quick readings and longer-term summaries from a manageable set of measurements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5835 defines temporal aggregation, spatial aggregation, and spatial composition, and requires metric definitions to state assumptions, applicability, and deviation from the ground truth.
tldr.outcome: The Informational framework covers composed packet-loss, delay, and delay-variation metrics. It treats composition of reordering and duplication metrics as research topics outside its scope.

facts.label: Composition classes
facts.value: Temporal aggregation, spatial aggregation, spatial composition

facts.label: Metric types in scope
facts.value: Packet loss, delay, and delay variation

today: RFC 5835 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Combine Measurements
sections.content:
The number of possible measurement paths grows with the square of the number of network nodes, so measuring every source-to-destination path can be impractical. An operator may measure along selected network segments and use those results to estimate performance across a larger path, accepting possible additional error.

Combining measurements can also reduce stored data and let short-term operational measurements support longer-term analysis. Spatial summaries can provide one value for a larger part of a network, while path composition can estimate performance across several connected networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring every possible path takes too many resources in a large network. Measurements of selected parts can be combined to estimate a larger view, with some possible loss of accuracy.

sections.title: Ground Truth and Composed Metrics
sections.content:
A complete-path metric is the actual source-to-destination measurement that a composed metric tries to estimate. The RFC calls that actual performance the ground truth. A composed metric is produced from other metrics by a deterministic composition function.

A sub-path is part of the complete path. If adjacent measurement endpoints are co-located and the link between them adds negligible performance, they may be treated as equivalent. If their connecting link affects performance, it should be measured as another sub-path.
sections.plainLanguage: The ground truth is the actual measurement for the whole path or period. A composed metric estimates that value by applying a defined calculation to measurements of parts.

sections.title: Three Ways to Compose Metrics
sections.content:
Temporal aggregation combines the same metric and scope across different time windows. The RFC's example takes the maximum of twelve consecutive five-minute maximum-delay measurements to obtain a sixty-minute maximum.

Spatial aggregation combines the same metric type across different scopes to summarize a larger network; inputs may be weighted. Spatial composition joins measurements of the same type over adjacent sub-paths, such as using measurements for A-to-B and B-to-C to estimate A-to-C. Unlike spatial aggregation, each sub-path contributes equally regardless of traffic load.
sections.plainLanguage: Temporal aggregation combines measurements from different time windows. Spatial aggregation summarizes different network areas, while spatial composition joins measurements from adjacent parts of a route.

sections.title: Assumptions, Missing Data and Error
sections.content:
A definition of a composed metric must state its definition, composition relationship, assumptions, practical use, ways the assumptions could be wrong, and reporting information. It must also explain applicable methods, measurement timing, independence assumptions, access requirements, and known sources of error.

Composed results can differ from ground truth because input errors propagate and measured sub-paths may not match the complete path exactly. A metric definition must describe that deviation. If a sub-path or time interval cannot be measured, the result should be recorded as undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: A metric definition needs to explain when its calculation works and how it could be wrong. If a required measurement is missing, record the result as undefined rather than inventing a value.
